subject: Financial Literacy
title: Priya's First Bank Account
hook: How can Priya keep her savings safe and make her money grow?

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Class 6 student starting to save seriously

characters.name: Harish (Priya's father)
characters.role: Takes Priya to open her first bank account

characters.name: Mr. Sharma (Bank Manager)
characters.role: Friendly bank manager who explains banking

slides.title: Banks — Where Money Stays Safe
slides.storyContext: Priya has saved ₹2000 under her pillow. One day her mother almost threw it away by mistake while cleaning. Priya's father says: 'Time to learn about banks. Your money will be safer there, and it will grow.'

image.alt: Banks — Where Money Stays Safe — Banks — Where Money Stays Safe

slides.title: Money Under the Pillow
slides.storyContext: Priya has been budgeting for 6 months and saved ₹2000 in a shoebox. One morning, her mother nearly gives it away with old clothes. Priya panics and calls her father. That weekend, he takes her to the State Bank of India branch near their house. 'Look,' her father says, 'banks keep money safer than any place at home. And your money earns interest while you keep it there. Let me show you.' They walk in, and Mr. Sharma, the friendly bank manager, greets them with tea and biscuits.

image.alt: Money Under the Pillow — Banks — Where Money Stays Safe

slides.title: What is a Bank?
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma opens a big book with the bank's name. 'A bank is a place where people keep money safe. We have strong vaults, guards, and computers. We are trusted by millions.' Priya feels the heavy wooden counter, imagining the vault inside.

points.label: Definition
points.text: A bank is a financial institution that accepts deposits (money from you) and keeps them safe in secure vaults.

points.label: Services
points.text: Banks offer accounts for saving, lending money, transfer of funds, and help with larger financial decisions.

points.label: Safety
points.text: Banks are regulated by the government (RBI—Reserve Bank of India). Your deposits up to ₹5 lakhs are insured by DICGC (deposit guarantee).

slides.inSimpleWords: A bank is a safe place to keep your money. The government watches banks to keep them trustworthy.

image.alt: What is a Bank? — Banks — Where Money Stays Safe

slides.title: Types of Bank Accounts
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma shows Priya three account types on a chart. 'For a student like you, a Savings Account is perfect. Let me explain each.'

points.label: Savings Account
points.text: For students and regular people. You deposit money, it stays safe, and you earn interest. You can withdraw anytime. Minimum balance ₹500–1000.

points.label: Current Account
points.text: For businesses and shop owners. Unlimited deposits and withdrawals, but no interest earned.

points.label: Fixed Deposit (FD)
points.text: You deposit money for a fixed time (6 months, 1 year, 5 years). You cannot withdraw early. Interest rate is higher. Priya will learn about FDs later.

example.problem: Priya wants to save ₹2000 safely and earn interest. She also needs to withdraw ₹500 after 2 months for her cricket camp. Which account type?
example.solution: Savings Account. She can keep ₹2000, earn interest, and withdraw ₹500 when needed without penalty.

slides.inSimpleWords: A Savings Account is for students who want to keep money safe, earn interest, and withdraw anytime.

image.alt: Types of Bank Accounts — Banks — Where Money Stays Safe

slides.title: Opening a Bank Account
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma hands Priya a form. 'You need three things: your birth certificate or Aadhaar, your school ID or passport, and a parent's signature because you are under 18. I will help you fill this.'

points.label: Documents
points.text: ID proof (Aadhaar, birth certificate, passport), Address proof (ration card, utility bill, school letter), Parent/guardian signature (because you are a minor).

points.label: Application
points.text: Fill the account opening form with your name, date of birth, address, contact number, and parent's details.

points.label: First Deposit
points.text: Deposit your starting amount (Priya deposits ₹2000). The bank issues a passbook or online account.

slides.inSimpleWords: To open a bank account: bring ID and parent, fill a form, deposit money. That is it!

image.alt: Opening a Bank Account — Banks — Where Money Stays Safe

slides.title: Interest: Your Money Grows
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'Mr. Sharma, will my ₹2000 stay ₹2000 forever?' He smiles. 'No, beta. Banks pay you interest. It is like a thank you for keeping your money with us. Every year, you earn extra money on top of your deposit.'

points.label: Interest
points.text: Money the bank pays you for keeping your deposit. Expressed as a percentage (e.g., 4% per annum).

points.label: Simple Interest Formula
points.text: Interest = (Principal × Rate × Time) / 100. Principal = amount deposited. Rate = interest % per year. Time = number of years.

points.label: Example
points.text: If Priya deposits ₹2000 at 4% interest for 1 year: Interest = (2000 × 4 × 1) / 100 = ₹80. After 1 year, she has ₹2080.

example.problem: Priya deposits ₹2000 in a Savings Account earning 4% per annum. What is the interest earned in 1 year? What is her total balance?
example.solution: Interest = (₹2000 × 4% × 1 year) / 100 = ₹80. Total balance after 1 year = ₹2000 + ₹80 = ₹2080.

slides.inSimpleWords: Banks pay you interest as a thank you for saving with them. Your money grows every year.

image.alt: Interest: Your Money Grows — Banks — Where Money Stays Safe

slides.title: Passbook and Statements
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma hands Priya a small, red passbook. 'Every time you deposit or withdraw, we write it here. You can come back anytime to see all your transactions. You can also check online on your phone now.' Priya opens it and sees the bank's stamp and her account number.

points.label: Passbook
points.text: A small booklet where the bank records every deposit, withdrawal, and interest credited. Physical proof of your account.

points.label: Account Number
points.text: A unique number for your account (e.g., 76543210001). Use this for deposits and transfers.

points.label: Online Banking
points.text: Banks now offer apps and websites. You can check balance, transfer money, pay bills, all from home.

slides.inSimpleWords: A passbook is your account's diary. It shows every rupee you put in, take out, and earn as interest.

image.alt: Passbook and Statements — Banks — Where Money Stays Safe

slides.title: Debit Card and Withdrawals
slides.storyContext: As Priya prepares to leave, Mr. Sharma gives her something else: a debit card. 'This is your debit card. You can use it to withdraw money from any ATM (Automated Teller Machine) in India, or pay for things in shops without carrying cash.' Priya holds it carefully, feeling very grown-up.

points.label: Debit Card
points.text: A card linked to your account. Use it to withdraw cash from ATMs or pay at shops (swipe or tap). Safe and convenient.

points.label: ATM
points.text: Machine available 24/7 outside or inside banks. Insert your debit card, enter PIN (secret 4-digit code), and withdraw cash.

points.label: PIN (Personal Identification Number)
points.text: A secret 4-digit code. NEVER share it with anyone, not even bank staff. Guard it like your password.

slides.inSimpleWords: A debit card lets you withdraw your money anytime from an ATM. Your PIN is your password—keep it secret.

image.alt: Debit Card and Withdrawals — Banks — Where Money Stays Safe

slides.title: Priya's First Year with the Bank
slides.storyContext: Priya opens her Savings Account with ₹2000 on 1 January. For 12 months, she continues to save ₹130 every month (from her budget!) and deposits it. At the end of the year, the bank credits interest. Let us calculate her total.

example.problem: Priya deposits ₹2000 on 1 January at 4% p.a. interest. She then deposits ₹130 every month for the next 11 months (Feb–Dec). The bank credits interest on the full amount at year-end. What is her total balance? (Simple interest on ₹2000 only for this exercise.)
example.solution: Initial deposit: ₹2000. Monthly deposits: ₹130 × 11 = ₹1430. Total deposited: ₹2000 + ₹1430 = ₹3430. Interest on ₹2000 for 1 year at 4% = (₹2000 × 4 × 1) / 100 = ₹80. Total balance = ₹3430 + ₹80 = ₹3510 after 1 year.

slides.inSimpleWords: Priya deposits regularly and earns interest. In one year, her ₹2000 grows to ₹3510—and she saved ₹1430 more!

image.alt: Priya's First Year with the Bank — Banks — Where Money Stays Safe

slides.title: Your Bank Account Challenge
slides.storyContext: You are now ready to open your own bank account. You have ₹1500 to start. Your bank offers 5% interest per annum. If you deposit ₹1500 and do not add or withdraw for 1 year, how much will you have at the end?

example.problem: You deposit ₹1500 at 5% p.a. interest for 1 year. No additional deposits. Calculate interest and final balance.

slides.inSimpleWords: To find how much your money grows: Interest = (Amount × Rate × Time) / 100. Add interest to your principal.

image.alt: Your Bank Account Challenge — Banks — Where Money Stays Safe

slides.title: Banks: Your Money's Best Friend
slides.storyContext: One year later, Priya sits in the bank with her passbook. Her ₹2000 has grown to ₹3510 through consistent saving and interest. Mr. Sharma shakes her hand. 'You learned the power of banking, Priya. By the time you are 18, you will have enough for college.'

points.text: A bank is a safe place for your money, protected by the government.
Savings Accounts are for students. You earn interest on deposits and can withdraw anytime.
Open an account with ID, address proof, and a parent's signature.
Interest = (Principal × Rate × Time) / 100. Your money grows every year.
Use debit cards and ATMs safely. Guard your PIN. Banking teaches discipline and builds wealth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Banks are safe. Save regularly. Earn interest. Your money grows. That is the bank's promise to you.

image.alt: Banks: Your Money's Best Friend — Banks — Where Money Stays Safe

subject: Mathematics
title: The Mystery of the Tiling Pattern
hook: Raj discovers repeating patterns in his grandmother's kitchen tiles—and learns the math hidden inside.

slides.title: Patterns in Mathematics
slides.storyContext: Raj and Priya visit their grandmother's house in a village. They notice the beautiful tiles on the kitchen floor follow a repeating design.

slides.title: A Puzzle on the Floor
slides.storyContext: Nani shows Raj and Priya the kitchen tiles: white, blue, white, blue, white, blue... They look like a simple pattern, but Nani asks: 'Can you predict the 10th tile without counting?'

slides.title: What Is a Pattern?
slides.storyContext: Nani explains that a pattern is something that repeats in a regular way—like the tiles.

points.label: A pattern
points.text: is a sequence where elements repeat in the same order

points.label: Example
points.text: white, blue, white, blue follows a pattern of 2 tiles that repeats

slides.inSimpleWords: A pattern is like a rule that tells you what comes next.

slides.title: Number Patterns: Odd Numbers
slides.storyContext: Nani asks: 'How many mangoes should we buy if we arrange them in odd rows: 1 mango, 3 mangoes, 5 mangoes, 7 mangoes...'

points.label: Rule
points.text: Each number is 2 more than the previous number

example.problem: What is the 5th odd number in the sequence?

slides.inSimpleWords: Odd numbers come in a pattern: add 2 to get the next one.

image.alt: Number Patterns: Odd Numbers — Patterns in Mathematics

slides.title: Even Number Patterns
slides.storyContext: Priya notices the rice bags at the market: 2 bags, 4 bags, 6 bags, 8 bags... 'This is a pattern too!' she says.

points.label: Rule
points.text: Even numbers increase by 2 every time

slides.inSimpleWords: Even numbers are: 2, 4, 6, 8... each 2 more than before.

slides.title: Multiplication Table Patterns
slides.storyContext: At school, Raj realizes the 3-times table on the wall follows a pattern: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18...

points.label: Pattern
points.text: Each number is 3 more than the number before it

slides.inSimpleWords: Times tables are patterns too—each row adds the same number each time.

slides.title: Square Numbers: A Growing Pattern
slides.storyContext: Raj arranges small stones in the courtyard: 1 stone in a square, then 4 stones (2×2), then 9 stones (3×3), then 16 stones (4×4).

points.label: Pattern
points.text: Each number is a perfect square

example.problem: What is the next square number after 25?

slides.inSimpleWords: Square numbers come from multiplying a number by itself: 3 × 3 = 9.

slides.title: Predicting the Next Tile
slides.storyContext: Now Raj can solve Nani's puzzle! The kitchen tiles are: white, blue, white, blue, white, blue...

points.label: Pattern type
points.text: The tiles alternate every position: odd positions are white, even positions are blue

points.label: The rule
points.text: Position 1: white, Position 2: blue, Position 3: white, Position 4: blue...

example.solution: Position 10 is even, so it's blue. Answer: blue

slides.inSimpleWords: By finding the pattern, you can predict anything in the sequence without counting.

slides.title: Can You Find the Pattern?
slides.storyContext: Nani challenges: 'Raj, here are some numbers: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25... What is the 7th number?'

example.problem: Find the 7th number in the pattern: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25...
example.solution: Pattern: add 5 each time. 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 → 7th number is 35

slides.inSimpleWords: Always look for what changes between numbers to find the pattern.

image.alt: Can You Find the Pattern? — Patterns in Mathematics

points.text: A pattern is something that repeats in a regular way
Odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, ... (add 2)
Even numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, ... (add 2)
Multiplication tables are patterns that add the same number
Square numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25... (perfect squares)
Once you find the rule, you can predict any number in the pattern

subject: Mathematics
title: Building the Kite Festival Stage
hook: During a kite festival, Raj and Priya build a stage using ropes and poles—and discover the angles hidden in everyday structures.

slides.title: Lines and Angles
slides.storyContext: It's kite festival season in Delhi. Raj and Priya's neighborhood is building a stage for the celebration, and Malik Uncle (a local carpenter) needs help arranging the beams and ropes.

image.alt: Lines and Angles — Lines and Angles

slides.title: The Perfect Stage
slides.storyContext: Malik Uncle explains: 'The stage needs a strong frame. I'll use straight beams (lines) and the way they meet (angles) will hold everything together. Do you understand?'

image.alt: The Perfect Stage — Lines and Angles

slides.title: What Is a Line?
slides.storyContext: Malik Uncle draws a chalk line on the ground. 'This line goes on and on forever in both directions—it has no start and no end.'

points.label: A line
points.text: is a straight path that extends infinitely in both directions

points.label: Symbol
points.text: Often shown with arrows on both ends: ←→

example.problem: Is a rope from the ground to the roof a line?
example.solution: No, it has two endpoints, so it's a line segment, not a line

slides.inSimpleWords: A line is perfectly straight and goes on forever.

image.alt: What Is a Line? — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Line Segments and Rays
slides.storyContext: Priya points at the stage poles: 'These aren't forever—they stop at the top!' Malik Uncle nods: 'Yes, those are line segments. And this flashlight beam? That's a ray—it has a start but goes on forever.'

points.label: Line segment
points.text: A straight path with two endpoints (like a pole)

points.label: Ray
points.text: A straight path with one starting point that goes on forever

slides.inSimpleWords: A segment has two ends. A ray has one end and goes forever.

image.alt: Line Segments and Rays — Lines and Angles

slides.title: What Is an Angle?
slides.storyContext: Two ropes meet at a corner of the stage. Malik Uncle says: 'The space between these two lines is called an angle. Let me measure it.'

points.label: An angle
points.text: is formed when two rays or line segments meet at a point (called the vertex)

points.label: Vertex
points.text: The point where the two lines meet

example.problem: Do two ropes lying flat on the ground form an angle?
example.solution: Only if they meet at a point. If they're separate, there's no angle

slides.inSimpleWords: An angle is the space opened up between two lines that meet.

image.alt: What Is an Angle? — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Types of Angles: Right Angle
slides.storyContext: Malik Uncle uses a square tool: 'When two beams meet at exactly 90 degrees, we call it a right angle. Like a corner of a book!'

points.label: Right angle
points.text: Measures exactly 90 degrees (written as 90°)

points.label: Symbol
points.text: A small square in the corner shows a right angle

points.label: Examples
points.text: Corner of a room, corner of a page, corner of this stage platform

example.problem: Is the corner of a cricket pitch a right angle?
example.solution: Yes—cricket fields are rectangular, so all corners are 90°

slides.inSimpleWords: A right angle looks like the corner of a square—exactly 90 degrees.

image.alt: Types of Angles: Right Angle — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Acute and Obtuse Angles
slides.storyContext: Priya arranges ropes at different angles. 'Malik Uncle, this rope makes a sharper angle than the right angle. And this one is wider!'

points.label: Acute angle
points.text: Less than 90° (smaller/sharper than a right angle)

points.label: Obtuse angle
points.text: More than 90° but less than 180° (wider than a right angle)

example.problem: Is a 45° angle acute or obtuse?
example.solution: 45° is less than 90°, so it's acute

slides.inSimpleWords: Acute is sharp and pointy. Obtuse is wide and open.

image.alt: Acute and Obtuse Angles — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Straight Angle and Reflex Angle
slides.storyContext: Malik Uncle extends two ropes in opposite directions: 'When the angle is exactly a straight line (180°), we call it a straight angle.'

points.label: Straight angle
points.text: Measures exactly 180° (a straight line)

points.label: Reflex angle
points.text: More than 180° but less than 360° (the larger angle on the other side)

slides.inSimpleWords: A straight angle is flat like a line. A reflex angle bends all the way around.

image.alt: Straight Angle and Reflex Angle — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Building a Perfect Corner
slides.storyContext: Now Raj and Priya help build the stage corner. Malik Uncle says: 'We need a right angle here. Let me check with my tool.'

example.problem: If two beams meet at 90°, what kind of angle is it?
example.solution: It's a right angle—perfect for a strong corner

slides.inSimpleWords: Right angles are the most common in buildings because they're strong and stable.

image.alt: Building a Perfect Corner — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Angle Detective
slides.storyContext: Malik Uncle challenges the kids: 'Look around the stage. Find one right angle, one acute angle, and one obtuse angle.'

example.problem: The corner of the stage is a right angle (90°). The open door makes an acute angle (about 45°). The staircase lean is obtuse (about 120°). Can you find these in your home?
example.solution: Right angle: corner of a room. Acute angle: half-open door. Obtuse angle: ladder against a wall

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles are everywhere—look for them in buildings, furniture, and nature.

image.alt: Angle Detective — Lines and Angles

points.text: A line extends forever in both directions
A line segment has two endpoints
A ray has one endpoint and extends forever
An angle is formed where two lines or rays meet
Right angle = 90°; Acute angle < 90°; Obtuse angle > 90°
Straight angle = 180°

image.alt: What You've Learned — Lines and Angles
